review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

After the success of [b]Sara Is Missing[/b], it was obvious [i]Kaigan Games[/i] would continue in the same vein of development. Truth is, before [b]Sara is Missing[/b], there was [b]Finding Home[/b], an indie game also simulating a smartphone experience. Seems the studio entire direction is surrounded by this peculiar genre, one that connects players into a stylized voyeur adventure never seen before.

In [b]SIMULACRA[/b] players gain access to a smartphone belonging to a young woman named Anna. She’s just like any other girl in her early 20’s, working and having a good time with her friends online and offline. All seems perfectly fine, except Anna went missing and she left a strange, bizarre video, as her last registered action.

The overall story is embedded within Anna’s online actions, and each new lead will reveal parts of her past, with phone backups and confessions from her friends. Dialogues are pretty realistic and interesting, making the overall experience more pleasant. There’s no drama, but it’s still somehow intense with a touch of horror and matching jump scares.

Players will explore Anna’s inner secrets and sneak peek into her life, as well as in her problems. Through smartphone apps, such as email, chats, and even the equivalent of Twitter and Tinder, we’ll meet her acquaintances and find clues that may lead to Anna’s whereabouts. While browsing text and pictures, we can restore them by either forming a phrase out of loose words, and building an image by restoring little pieces at a time.

Finding Anna is as much part of the story, as create a connection with other persons of interest through social media. You’ll have to find clues and discover ways to connect with others, to collect new information. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] allows you to open up, or, in some cases, keep pretending to be Anna, which may open up new dialogue options and information.

There’s a certain acquired taste when going through someone else’s life, and the game clearly explores that with decency, but still waving a round or two of peculiar situations and encounters. Some internet references and expressions can be found all over the place, adding a certain style and characterization of realism into that social media life.

It’s one of those experiences, where you’ll forget you’re in the game. As soon as the clues start rolling down and the story involving, it’s a fantastic journey. Gathering clues and finding the direction to go was always relatively easy, and I never found myself stuck or without an idea of where to go. The game also contains a section with the objectives, which will help out in most scenarios if needed.

The visual presentation is accurate and suiting. It’s far more comfortable browsing this virtual phone, then rather use a phone in real life obviously, since the game grants resolutions up to your own. Videos and pictures follow the expected quality and it’s an authentic experience as far as design goes.

Indie games featuring live-action performances with quality are rare. Most of the times the studio goes to an alternative or stylized acting. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] though, doesn’t need any of those tricks, and [url=www.instagram.com/wendyvanhoren/]Wendy Van Horen[/url] plays Anna surprisingly well. Some may claim it’s an amateurish act, but remember, this is Anna’s life, a young person sharing vlogs about her personal life experiences. Wendy definitely brings the character alive, adding a natural and realistic touch.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] dwells between our presence in the real world, versus our digital personas. I personally think it’s a really good concept and it’s well depict. Doesn’t become far-fetched, even when dealing with the supernatural. It’s a horror experience, but more towards what social media means to us, and how scary it can become. Very entertaining and for the simple price of $3,99 it’s impossible to avoid recommending this one.

[h1]A First Impression Review[/h1]

I shouldn't have liked this, but I did. I'm not a horror fan, but the concept was interesting enough to keep me hooked. It reminds me of the movie [i]Smile[/i]. It’s creepy and has some jumpscares that make you feel uncomfortable, but the intrigue of the puzzles actually sold me, despite not being a puzzle guy.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- [b]Realistic Interface:[/b] Feels exactly like operating a normal Android phone. It's natural and easy to navigate.
- [b]Clever Puzzles:[/b] The difficulty is just right. You have to really think, like hunting through emails to find a mother’s maiden name for a password reset. 
- [b]The Drama:[/b] There is a good chunk of backstory in the messages. Reading through the texts, like the drama with the mom, felt realistic and wild. It adds weight to the mystery. It actually made me care about the missing women. 
- [b]Great Price:[/b] This game is cheap. It's under $10 at full price, and catching it on sale for under $2 is a big W.
- [b]Good Pacing:[/b] The game pushes you in the right direction. If you finish a task, you’ll get an alert letting you know exactly which app or person to investigate next.

[h1]The Not-So-Good[/h1]
- [b]Awkward Acting:[/b] The acting is a little awkward at times. I definitely laughed at a few moments, but it gets the job done and sells the story.

[b]TLDR:[/b] A neat mystery that makes you want to keep playing to see what happens next. If you like unique puzzles and can handle a bit of a creep factor, it’s worth it.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
☐ Skip It
☐ Buy it on Sale
☑️ Worth it at Full Price

review_text_raw:
After playing Sara is Missing and hearing about Simulacra through that purveyor of all things horror-related, Night Mind, I decided to check it out.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The story is much more developed compared to SiM, and I enjoyed exploring Anna's phone.  The concept of the game was much more interesting than SiM, though I feel like it could still be better developed and hope the devs continue with this idea.  While the text speak used by the main "players" of the game was perfectly realistic, I felt that the primary antagonist of the game [spoiler]Simulacra[/spoiler] would not have the spelling errors I encountered in that character's texting.  For instance, the character used "lead" instead of "led" and "it's" when "its" was intended.  I know, I know, others might not have noticed or been affected by this, but I felt that the character would not have made those errors.

Overall, the characters were better developed than SiM, definitely.  Anna was three-dimensional, and so were the characters we encountered.  Omitting Iris [spoiler]though of course allusions can be found in the website, thanks to the phone number and Morse Code[/spoiler], was a good decision.  I don't know if the plan is for DLC or sequels, but I look forward to a continuation of the Simulacra and/or Iris story-line, in this world where technology has a mind of its own.

For the devs:
[list]
[*]The ambiance is brilliant.  I love the room behind the phone, the lights flickering and the sounds around me.  It definitely creates an aura of suspense.
[*]As far as jump scares, I agree with Night Mind, unnecessary, kind of lame, and ineffective.
[*]What did solving the puzzles accomplish?  I mean, I don't know if I had to unscramble the photos and texts to progress, I just always do it to get it out of the way, but they don't, in the story, progress anything, really, [spoiler]until the Spark conversation with James[/spoiler].  Also they were really easy.  When you present me with a four-word scramble...come on.
[*]Where is this supposed to take place?  The accents were peculiar.  It seemed like you were aiming for American, but you were using British spellings, i.e. favourite.  Is it meant to take place in Canada?
[*]I did love the multiple endings, and felt much more invested in them than I did in SiM.  In particular, [spoiler]I just achieved the happy ending, and afterward, stared at the screen and said, "Did I just get possessed?  I think I just got possessed."[/spoiler]
[*][spoiler]Even if you're interviewing through text (for reasons?), why would you consider hiring a person to be a copywriter who makes that many spelling and grammatical errors?  I kept looking at my response options, and they were painful.  Yes, I understand you're not really applying and just trying to get information about James, but still.[/spoiler]
[/list]
All that being said, I do hope you continue and would love to play any other games set in this world.  If you appreciate nothing else from my review, let it be: less is more.  Subtle horror is better than overt horror.  The idea that somebody might be in the room with you, where you're holding that phone, or the idea that you might lower the phone and see, I don't know, a floating disembodied head, was so much more effective than momentary flashes of the screen turning into something scary.  And if [spoiler]the final image had been the player lowering the screen and something vague and shadowy, or even a representation of the Simulacra, being there, and then moving toward the screen if you simply must jump scare, it would have been better than the shift in Anna's picture.[/spoiler]  It's the suspense that gets you, not the actual scare.  You don't have the suspense before the jump scares on the phone, just an image shift.

Nevertheless, public who have reached this far (or TLDR), I do recommend this game.  It isn't a long game, but I've spent...7 hours in it so far?  And intend to spend more unlocking achievements.

There's a sub-genre of games that I like to call voyeur sims -- these include walking simulators like Gone Home, strategy-puzzlers like the Orwell games, and story-driven phone-sim games like [b]SIMULACRA[/b].

These voyeur sims fuel something visceral in me by allowing me to be a peeping tom in someone else's life; overcoming personal privacy as a game mechanic is somehow uncomfortably fun, even when the actual gameplay is minimal.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] is one of the better voyeur sims and one of the better games I've played this year. Like other phone-sim games like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/523210/A_Normal_Lost_Phone/]A Normal Lost Phone[/url] and [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/496890/Replica/]Replica[/url], it starts with a mysterious cell phone, and throughout the game, you unpack its content in a series of puzzle-driven unlocking sequences.

What sets [b]SIMULACRA[/b] apart is its high production value. High quality FMVs, passable and explorable versions of popular social media apps, realistic text logs and emails -- these all make the small, contained world of [b]SIMULACRA[/b] believable and immersive.

This is a great game. Recommended.

I got this game today and I was incredibly excited to play. I did around 4 playthroughs, trying to see the easter eggs and gather all the achievements and overall I'm rather amazed.

The use of real people in a game was a new concept to me but I enjoyed the idea a lot, especially since it highlighted the possible dangers of the digital world and made them more transferrable to the real world. The voice acting was a bit unrealistic sometimes but that's a minor issue. 

There are 5 possible endings (though the game at the end shows you only four of them) and your choices really impact them. The dialogue options that the game revolves around either make or break your case, so you have to think about what to choose.

The game is rather easy, in most cases if you get stuck at anything either of the two characters that you keep talking to will help you. 

After over 6 hours of playthrough, I have to say I am really impressed with this game. It was my first time ever playing something of this format and I will now have expectations for the future. I would not count this game as a horror, since the repeated jumpscares and glitches were far from scary (but maybe they might scare some people, who knows!). The true scary theme in the game is the realization that people on the Internet might really be bad and you shouldn't trust everyone you meet online. 

Even though it's common knowledge, when showcased like this, it can be eye-opening to some. Great game.

review_text_raw:
I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. 

That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact.

[h2] Music [/h2]
There isn't as much to gush about here. I'd say it does its job and the title screen is iconic.Part of me wishes I had some more songs to add to my gamer Main Character Syndrome Spotify playlist, but I also do think limiting the soundtrack and sticking to eiry silence cut off by that terrifying sound design is the way to go.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
If I ever found a missing person's phone, and everyone treated me like this, I'd either 1. Say she's better off missing or 2. Just hand the phone off to the cops. 

[h3] Anna [/h3]
They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic!

Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Be told by everyone how important it is to hunt him down and bring him back, slowly uncovering that he's not that great of a person, having to contemplate with the consequences of what it would mean to actually bring the jerk back. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. 

[h3] Taylor [/h3]
He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. That's a lot of work for cardboard you saw on sale on Ebay. 

[h3] Greg [/h3]
People like to rip on the actor for this guy, and yeah, I get it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be laughing at him or if he was supposed to tick me off or if heaven forbid he was supposed to scare me, but he did two of three (i'm sure you can guess which ones). I think Greg sees Anna as someone who he can easily control and manipulate. Which makes sense. She is cardboard. I did find it odd on one route where he [spoiler] suddenly abandons pursuing Anna as soon as he learns the cops are after him [/spoiler]. It came out of left field and then you never learn what happens to him from that point. Honestly, I love to hate Greg, so I think he does his job. I can understand him being obsessive over Anna since 1. they dated for two years and 2. she sees her as easy. 

[h3] Ashley [/h3]
THIS GIRL TICKED ME OFF. I'm not talking about the route where you [spoiler] lie to her and manipulate her into saying she's in love with Anna, though again I ask WHY [/spoiler]. I'm talking about how she treats you if you come clean right away and just tell her who you are and why you have Anna's phone. She flips, gets super defensive. won't let you explain yourself, and then calls the cops on you. She'll randomly disappear from the plot and go offline, and she won't work with you no matter what you say to her. I find that highly improbable. I don't think they knew what to do with Ashley for the routes where [spoiler] she knows the truth [/spoiler].

[h3] Everyone else [/h3]
Nothing much to report. No one made me as mad as Anna's supposed BFF. So good job.

[h3] Simulacra [/h3]
Alright, I have an issue. This thing isn't scary. There's so much buildup, then it's just kind of there. It's so melodramatic and easy to make fun of. I almost think this story would've been better of Greg had just killed her or something. I don't understand how this thing kills or kidnaps, I'm not scared of it, and it keeps changing the rules. I dunno, I just wanted one last big scare, or something that felt satisfying after all that buildup. Then I saw it, and I thought, that's it?

[h2] Story [/h2]
In this game you find a phone that is clearly possessed, and are tasked to find its owner, Anna. You are helped and hindered by the various people trying to get ahold of her, and you can either leave her life in shambles for her to return to or make her life better with your interference. 

Some aspects were rewarding. I liked getting to put that one workplace creep in his place. I liked when I got her a new job in that one playthrough.

I think the main issues with the story were already discussed in the characters section. I don't think the payoff was satisfying. I think I see what they are going for, with the good ending that is. You have to become a master manipulator to take down the manipulator, I do like that. Again, I just felt like the final boss was an absolute joke. I thought it was fake, there was another boss behind the boss, or something. I think the plot excels in relationship drama and just making terrible people act terrible. It's guilty pleasure level entertaining. It gets lost in the big ideas and trying to be bigger than it actually is. I think if it had stuck to a nitty gritty found phone horror game, with people as its worst enemy, it would've stuck the landing a bit more.

[h2] Theme [/h2]
Dating apps bad. Something about valuing the real world over the virtual. Game certainly doesn't punish you much for becoming a master online troll catfishing manipulator. But maybe...maybe that's the real point. We can look back at a preinternet time and recognize that certain things were better back then. But the fact of the matter is, that world doesn't exist anymore. 

Wow. That went deeper than I thought. Too bad the villian sucks and I don't care about Anna. 

[h1] Wait, didn't you recommend this game? I'm confused [/h1]
Yes. I do.

I think it's fun. Fun like watching the Scream franchise. Fun like a haunted hayride sponsored by a high school, where you know things are corny, but you know what, for those couple of times they made you jump, it was worth spending a couple bucks for a ride. Just wait for a Steam sale and get it for like a dollar like I did. This was a really well spent dollar.

Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact. [h2] Music [/h2] There isn't as much to gush about here. I'd say it does its job and the title screen is iconic.Part of me wishes I had some more songs to add to my gamer Main Character Syndrome Spotify playlist, but I also do think limiting the soundtrack and sticking to eiry silence cut off by that terrifying sound design is the way to go. [h2] Characters [/h2] If I ever found a missing person's phone, and everyone treated me like this, I'd either 1. Say she's better off missing or 2. Just hand the phone off to the cops. [h3] Anna [/h3] They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic! Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Be told by everyone how important it is to hunt him down and bring him back, slowly uncovering that he's not that great of a person, having to contemplate with the consequences of what it would mean to actually bring the jerk back. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. [h3] Taylor [/h3] He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. That's a lot of work for cardboard you saw on sale on Ebay. [h3] Greg [/h3] People like to rip on the actor for this guy, and yeah, I get it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be laughing at him or if he was supposed to tick me off or if heaven forbid he was supposed to scare me, but he did two of three (i'm sure you can guess which ones). I think Greg sees Anna as someone who he can easily control and manipulate. Which makes sense. She is cardboard. I did find it odd on one route where he [spoiler] suddenly abandons pursuing Anna as soon as he learns the cops are after him [/spoiler]. It came out of left field and then you never learn what happens to him from that point. Honestly, I love to hate Greg, so I think he does his job. I can understand him being obsessive over Anna since 1. they dated for two years and 2. she sees her as easy. [h3] Ashley [/h3] THIS GIRL TICKED ME OFF. I'm not talking about the route where you [spoiler] lie to her and manipulate her into saying she's in love with Anna, though again I ask WHY [/spoiler]. I'm talking about how she treats you if you come clean right away and just tell her who you are and why you have Anna's phone. She flips, gets super defensive. won't let you explain yourself, and then calls the cops on you. She'll randomly disappear from the plot and go offline, and she won't work with you no matter what you say to her. I find that highly improbable. I don't think they knew what to do with Ashley for the routes where [spoiler] she knows the truth [/spoiler]. [h3] Everyone else [/h3] Nothing much to report. No one made me as mad as Anna's supposed BFF. So good job. [h3] Simulacra [/h3] Alright, I have an issue. This thing isn't scary. There's so much buildup, then it's just kind of there. It's so melodramatic and easy to make fun of. I almost think this story would've been better of Greg had just killed her or something. I don't understand how this thing kills or kidnaps, I'm not scared of it, and it keeps changing the rules. I dunno, I just wanted one last big scare, or something that felt satisfying after all that buildup. Then I saw it, and I thought, that's it? [h2] Story [/h2] In this game you find a phone that is clearly possessed, and are tasked to find its owner, Anna. You are helped and hindered by the various people trying to get ahold of her, and you can either leave her life in shambles for her to return to or make her life better with your interference. Some aspects were rewarding. I liked getting to put that one workplace creep in his place. I liked when I got her a new job in that one playthrough. I think the main issues with the story were already discussed in the characters section. I don't think the payoff was satisfying. I think I see what they are going for, with the good ending that is. You have to become a master manipulator to take down the manipulator, I do like that. Again, I just felt like the final boss was an absolute joke. I thought it was fake, there was another boss behind the boss, or something. I think the plot excels in relationship drama and just making terrible people act terrible. It's guilty pleasure level entertaining. It gets lost in the big ideas and trying to be bigger than it actually is. I think if it had stuck to a nitty gritty found phone horror game, with people as its worst enemy, it would've stuck the landing a bit more. [h2] Theme [/h2] Dating apps bad. Something about valuing the real world over the virtual. Game certainly doesn't punish you much for becoming a master online troll catfishing manipulator. But maybe...maybe that's the real point. We can look back at a preinternet time and recognize that certain things were better back then. But the fact of the matter is, that world doesn't exist anymore. Wow. That went deeper than I thought. Too bad the villian sucks and I don't care about Anna. [h1] Wait, didn't you recommend this game? I'm confused [/h1] Yes. I do. I think it's fun. Fun like watching the Scream franchise. Fun like a haunted hayride sponsored by a high school, where you know things are corny, but you know what, for those couple of times they made you jump, it was worth spending a couple bucks for a ride. Just wait for a Steam sale and get it for like a dollar like I did. This was a really well spent dollar.

A decent puzzle type game. While there are the occasional mild jump scares and something strange going on, it didn't really give me a horror or suspense vibe.

Pros:
- I generally stay away from FMV games, but the actresses & voice actors are actually pretty good
- The puzzle difficulty is OK for the most part
- Several other easter eggs and hidden puzzles if you want an extra challenge
- Has a mode for replaying to make text speed up instead of being at a realistic speed

Cons:
- Lacking in horror, and didn't feel that suspenseful
- Texts and responses when texting are often not quite right - grammatically wrong or just don't completely make sense. It could have used some more polish.
- Setting aside the fact that you're going through a stranger's phone instead of giving it to the police/family/etc, there are still things you have to do to progress the story that I would never think to do IRL
- While you frequently have different options for responses to messages, responses to what you say are frequently reused, giving the illusion of more choice than you really have. Good for role playing, but noticeable when replaying
- Has mutually exclusive achievements and different endings, but lacks replayability. Yes you can choose different dialogue option that can influence people differently, but the puzzles and their solutions are still the same.
- I wasn't a big fan of the ending. It didn't make much sense and wasn't really explained. That may have been saved for the second game though.

Verdict: 7/10

Wow… just wow. This game is really really really good. I didn’t expect it to be that good! 

Honestly, I don’t play much games of this genre. The first one was “Her story”. And this one is similar but waaaaay better.

You found the phone of Ana and need to message her contacts in various apps and use hints in chats and websites to find out what happened to her (she disappeared). 

The riddles are great (I especially enjoyed the one where I had to find cassie’s phone number), the smartphone control is smooth and realistic, the chats are interesting and humorous, and the story was compelling.

It made me want to play Simulacra 2. I must buy it now… But before playing the second one: As I enjoyed Simulacra so much and because I know that there are various endings, I will have to replay this game at least once to take different decisions.

[h1]👍 Highly Recommended[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA is one of the few games that genuinely makes browsing through a smartphone feel fun. It's a horror game of sorts, but Instead of running from monsters or hiding in closets, you're piecing together the disappearance of a young woman by exploring every corner of her phone. Messages, photos, videos, emails, social media, and browser history slowly reveal a mystery that's equal parts psychological thriller and supernatural horror. It feels disturbingly believable-almost like scrolling through someone else's real device.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🟢 PROS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Brilliant Found Phone Concept:[/b] Investigating an entire mystery through a lost smartphone is an incredibly immersive idea that still feels unique years after release.
[*][b]Excellent Storytelling:[/b] The narrative unfolds naturally through text messages, emails, videos, and social media instead of lengthy exposition. Every app contains another piece of the puzzle.
[*][b]Convincing Characters:[/b] Conversations feel surprisingly authentic. Friends, coworkers, and family all have believable personalities and motivations, making the investigation feel personal.
[*][b]Genuinely Creepy:[/b] SIMULACRA builds tension through unsettling discoveries, disturbing videos, and the feeling that something is deeply wrong with the phone itself.
[*][b]Creative Puzzles:[/b] Unlocking files, recovering deleted data, solving passwords, and navigating fake apps keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.
[*][b]Multiple Endings:[/b] Your decisions matter, giving the story additional replay value.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🔴 CONS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Live-Action Acting Can Be Uneven:[/b] Most performances are convincing, but a handful of scenes feel slightly awkward compared to the otherwise strong production.
[*][b]Occasional Interface Frustrations:[/b] Searching through apps or revisiting conversations can sometimes be more cumbersome than necessary.
[*][b]The Ending May Divide Players:[/b] Without spoilers, the final revelations won't satisfy everyone, especially those hoping for a more grounded explanation.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]💰 VALUE FOR MONEY[/h2]
[b]Excellent[/b] — SIMULACRA offers several hours of engaging investigation packed with memorable moments, clever puzzles, and one of the most original horror concepts in the genre. It's frequently discounted on Steam, making it an even easier recommendation for fans of narrative adventures and psychological horror.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]⭐ 9/10[/h3]
[i]A brilliantly executed smartphone horror that proves the scariest place in a horror game isn't an abandoned mansion. Immersive, unsettling, and remarkably original, SIMULACRA remains one of the most engaging narrative horror experiences available on Steam.[/i]

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good. 

You can find my curator page here: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Synik_GR

A decent puzzle type game. While there are the occasional mild jump scares and something strange going on, it didn't really give me a horror or suspense vibe.

Pros:
- I generally stay away from FMV games, but the actresses & voice actors are actually pretty good
- The puzzle difficulty is OK for the most part
- Several other easter eggs and hidden puzzles if you want an extra challenge
- Has a mode for replaying to make text speed up instead of being at a realistic speed

Cons:
- Lacking in horror, and didn't feel that suspenseful
- Texts and responses when texting are often not quite right - grammatically wrong or just don't completely make sense. It could have used some more polish.
- Setting aside the fact that you're going through a stranger's phone instead of giving it to the police/family/etc, there are still things you have to do to progress the story that I would never think to do IRL
- While you frequently have different options for responses to messages, responses to what you say are frequently reused, giving the illusion of more choice than you really have. Good for role playing, but noticeable when replaying
- Has mutually exclusive achievements and different endings, but lacks replayability. Yes you can choose different dialogue option that can influence people differently, but the puzzles and their solutions are still the same.
- I wasn't a big fan of the ending. It didn't make much sense and wasn't really explained. That may have been saved for the second game though.

Verdict: 7/10

I watched a playthrough of this game back in 2018, and I remember really liking it back then! When I was reminded of it's existence and heard positive buzz around it, I decided to try my hand at it. It is rather dated in some ways - the inclusion of a Twitter parody app, for one, and even the way characters post on that app scream early 2010's, and the other ways it's aged are just simply Millenialcore humor throughout - it also has quite a few typos (some more distracting than others), some of the voice acting is rough ("fuuuuuck thiiis sooooo muuuuuch" is now a repeated reference in my friend group for the absolutely baffling delivery lol). The plot and gimmicks are also rather predictable if you're at all familiar with this sub genre of horror media and akin sub genres. I recall the plot beats and phone gimmick/framing device being somewhat novel back in 2018, but maybe I misremember.

All that being said, I do enjoy this game and I think it's still worth playing! Some of my favorite things about this game are the soundscape (particularly the knocking and breathing noises randomly interspersed throughout), the interactivity and surprisingly accurate app design/aesthetics for some of the apps also helped immerse me, and I found myself very endeared to Anna and Ashley. This game is no masterpiece, but it's alright for what it is. I'd recommend you play it with a couple friends on voice call - y'all will have a good time leaving nonsense comments on the Jabbr posts, bullying Greg, being irked by Taylor, and making a bizarre dating profile!

review_text_raw:
It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

review_text_raw:
A fun, innovative experience involving navigating someone’s digital life to find out what happened to someone.

Background: I like playing interactive stories like this while I’m eating instead of watching TV or a movie. It’s good to play these kinds of games between bites.

I didn’t know what to make of this game—I think I got it as part of a bundle—but installed it and tried it out after running through a few movie games and wanting to shift to something else. I was pleasantly surprised by the story, and the gameplay was similar to games like Her Story and Orwell where you interact with a digital interface to make the story unfold.

The Positives:
-It really does feel like you are a person who found a phone and are trying to find out what happened to the owner. There are a few times where it is imperfect in terms of what you probably could/should/would do, but it does a good enough job that it felt realistic enough to suspend disbelief for several hours.

-The phone was fun to play around with—you go into various apps and learn about the owner’s recent activity and then even get to participate a little.

-The people you interact with are sketchy as hell, but it definitely made things interesting.

-The ending got pretty wild; while the horror elements are minimal for most of the game, the ending combines the genres of tech-thrillers and evil-spirit-horror—very interesting. It’s not simply like System Shock 2 or Terminator (where the tech tries to control you) or Evil Dead or The Ring (where evil spirits are trying to kill you); it’s an interesting mix.

-The people involved did a great job—there are a lot of photos, videos, and conversations, and both the actors and the developers did a great job of making it all fit together. It all felt real—I never thought for a moment that the photos or videos were “fake” or “made-for-the-game”. That’s all I look for in acting; not everything has to be Meryl Streep, and this felt real enough.

-The ending was fresh for me—the combination of it being just slightly different from other endings in the genre along with the uniqueness of me having to make decisions that led to the outcome made the experience very new and interesting.

The Negatives:
-As I mentioned, the people you interact with are sketchy, which I overall enjoyed but it does result in some weird interactions. I thought it worked, but I wouldn’t be surprised if you played and said, “Why don’t they just do X?” — I felt that any plot holes were covered up well enough for me to buy it, but you might not.

-If you like a lot of horror, there isn’t much here—it ratchets up near the end but for the most part is more of a mystery with a dash of spooky/thriller elements. I liked the amount, but you might want more.

-It’s tough to strike a balance between elements that build the character and world with ones that begin to give you hints about the mystery…I think they did a good job, but you might find that early on you go through a lot of videos and photos that don’t reveal much. The photos are easy enough to skim through, but you’ll watch several videos and they don’t really do much other than give you a live look at what the owner looked like while slowly introducing the fact that something is amiss. If you’re a narrative critic, you’d probably want them to have done more with those elements than just a look into the life of the owner.

Overall, it’s an interesting game. I was engaged most of the time and there are only brief periods where there is a lot of text back-and-forth that you might want something more to be happening—but it’s not bad by any means. If you are sucked in at those points, you will enjoy it. If not, that’s probably where you might tune out. The good news is that the developers listened and put in the ability to adjust the speed, etc. of the game (especially if you’re replaying it) to solve for that issue. So I think you’ll be okay. As long as you like the mysterious look-into-the-life-of-someone-else genre of point-and-click games (like the “found footage” genre of movies but for video games), you’ll enjoy it. If you are hoping for a lot of horror, though, there isn’t too much and so I just hope to set your expectations appropriately.

At the time of its release, I was kind of obsessed with Sara is Missing. The style was fresh and new, and what a great idea! Finding a missing person through their phone is already such an interesting mystery, a look at how much of our lives are stored in this technology with a personal touch. However, in the end, I had too many questions that went unanswered, and ultimately felt unsatisfied.

SIMULACRA, on the other hand, has so far fixed all of these issues. For clarity sake, I have only achieved two endings at this time, and have more to go. For the same reason, and to give my respect to the developers, I will say I found this game through NightMind's video. This was one of the very, very few times I actually paused in the middle of a video to go out and buy the game myself - I will admit however, the low price was a factor in that. I was expecting more, but this game was more than worth my money.

There are a few silly little mistakes - Some of which add a level of realism and are undoubtedly intentional, like the varying type styles and occasional grammar errors and misspells... And some which are just a little funny, but in the end, the writing and acting won me over any time I was distracted from the experience. The mystery this time around is far more fun and rewarding to solve, the characters are largely likable (UNLESSANNAWHEREARETHOSEDATAREPORTS) and believable within this context.

The whole theme of using someone's phone to dig through their identity is played with far, FAR more effectively here, and the paranormal aspects (cmon it was obvious) offer some commentary, as well as another interesting character I wanted to explore.

The fact that the game doesn't allow multiple save states to allow choice-scumming for the desired result was at first a bit annoying, I want to see what they would all say if I said this or that, but it does add a certain weight to each choice - If you slip up and don't want to see it through, you have to start over.

There are a few other fun little distractions, if you need a moment of relief from the spooks, such as replying over and over again to the home security bot, replying to other people's tweets with memes, editing Anna's Spark profile the moment you have access to it so that it shows the lyrics to Feel Good Inc. and a picture of her cat, and etc. And even if you do choose to mess around a little it, you can still progress the story whether or not Anna's profile name is now Snart.

While I can't promise poo your pants horror, and the scares will be subjective, it's a fun little game even if you only want to pretend to be another person and gain everyone's trust, or immediately tell everyone you meet that you're not Anna. Or call 911, call her friends, read her texts and emails, waste her phone battery, and etc.

The fact that the game doesn't allow multiple save states to allow choice-scumming for the desired result was at first a bit annoying, I want to see what they would all say if I said this or that, but it does add a certain weight to each choice - If you slip up and don't want to see it through, you have to start over. There are a few other fun little distractions, if you need a moment of relief from the spooks, such as replying over and over again to the home security bot, replying to other people's tweets with memes, editing Anna's Spark profile the moment you have access to it so that it shows the lyrics to Feel Good Inc. and a picture of her cat, and etc. And even if you do choose to mess around a little it, you can still progress the story whether or not Anna's profile name is now Snart. While I can't promise poo your pants horror, and the scares will be subjective, it's a fun little game even if you only want to pretend to be another person and gain everyone's trust, or immediately tell everyone you meet that you're not Anna. review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone simulator. Apparently that's a genre now. 

On a phone, the premise of Simulacra is something special: What if your phone turned into someone else's phone, and you could hack into it to snoop out all the little things about our life that we entrust to our phones these days. And because said phone gives you complete access to the online persona of the owner of that phone, you also get to moonlight as an online predator. 

It still works well enough on the PC, although the immersion is somewhat diminished. 

But hey, it's OK, because Anna, the owner of the phone, is in trouble and you are the only one with access to enough information to maybe help her. And also…  this is just a game. 

If I sound like I'm down on the game for the icky things it expects you to do, I'm actually not. The game never shies away from pointing out how questionable the means you employ are, and if you want it, you can go about things in the most ethical way possible. You won't get the best ending, though. 

The actual means by which the game let's you morally compromise yourself are quite simple. Some light social hacking, catfishing, actual hacking, two simple mini-games. The rest of the time you read dialogue or watch a few videos with above average novice actors, and thus follow along a nifty little horror story whose ending felt very rushed but still packed quite a punch. 

The game is a bit railroady, though. The main thing you do is converse with Anna's contacts via multiple choice chat, and oftentimes the few options you have are very obviously pushing the story in the direction it wants to go. Thanks to the brevity of the game, this never gets too grating, though. 

The main freight of meaning and engagement this game transported for me was the fun and glee you can actually get out of pretending to be a terrible person with access to someone else's phone, and thinking about what that actually means for the hellscape we are all constructing for ourselves. There is no way around it: If you have no moral compass, being a troll is a very good time. Good thing then that in Simulacra, the moral justification comes with the box. 

TLDR: Interesting little title whose premise and insinuations become more horrifying the longer you think about it. Bit on the short side, but well worth experiencing.

SIMULACRA scared the absolute crap out of me, and that’s one of the biggest compliments I can give a horror game. The entire game takes place through a missing person’s phone, which creates a unique and immersive experience that feels unsettlingly realistic.

What makes SIMULACRA so effective is how believable everything feels. You’re scrolling through messages, watching videos, checking social media, and uncovering clues while trying to figure out what happened. As the story progresses, things become increasingly disturbing, and there were multiple moments that genuinely made me uncomfortable in the best possible way.

The game does an excellent job building tension and mystery, making it hard to put down once you start uncovering the truth. The live-action performances help sell the story, and the feeling that something is constantly watching or manipulating events keeps you on edge throughout the entire experience.

Overall, SIMULACRA is an amazing horror game that delivers both great scares and an engaging mystery. If you’re looking for a horror experience that feels different from the usual formula, I highly recommend it.

Rating: 9/10

A genuinely creepy and immersive horror game that had me hooked from beginning to end and scared me more than I expected.

review_text_raw:
I'm a huge fan of this kind of voyeuristic mystery genre, and this is one of the best I've come across. 
The mixing of platforms; text, audio and FMV, creates a very realistic and immersive phone to explore. The level of detail inside the phone apps is also unparallelled. You can explore people's profiles on the dating app and strike up a conversation with someone inconsequential, you can read comments on posts on the social media app, you can read spam emails. So much detail was put into building the world.
The characters (while the voice and visual acting can be a little hokey) each have their own distinct personalities through texts and messages, the writing there is spot on, plus you can interact with them in so many different ways it feels like your voice really matters to the plot.   
I was put off this game initially because I'm a huge wimp and not a big horror fan, but the scares never made me want to stop playing, and it was really worth it.
11/10 I can't wait for the next game from these guys.
